scenarios.name: Tampered
scenarios.line: 200 in 167 ms · accepted a changed body

signing.kind: signed for the original body, fresh timestamp

request.bodyNote: amount_paid edited in place 2400 → 0 (no re-serialisation, Content-Length recomputed); Stripe-Signature computed for the original body at a fresh timestamp

findings.title: Accepts tampered payload
findings.what: D12 changed amount_paid from 2400 to 0 and was signed for the original body. Your handler returned 200 in 167 ms and created an order: orders.count 0 → 1, expected a 4xx and no change.
findings.why: Stripe signs the exact bytes it sends. If a failed check doesn't stop the request, anyone who can reach this URL can create paid orders.

fix.text: Return 400 as soon as constructEvent throws, before any write. After the fix, D12 should get 400 and leave orders.count at 0.

likelyCause.text: Late (D9) was rejected, so the timestamp check runs; the signature check probably fails into a log line instead of stopping the request.

findings.measured: HTTP 200 in 167 ms · orders.count 0 → 1 · expected: a 4xx and no change

findings.title: Duplicate delivery created a second order
findings.what: D5 delivered the same invoice.paid event as D4. Both got 200 {"received":true}, but orders.count went 1 → 2, expected 1. The retry D11 did the same after D10. Only the probe could see this.
findings.why: Stripe may deliver the same event more than once, and retries failed or timed-out deliveries with backoff for up to 3 days in live mode. Each duplicate creates another order.

citation.label: Stripe docs › Webhooks › Handle duplicate events · Retry behavior

fix.text: Record event.id before creating the order and return 200 early when it is already recorded. After the fix, D5 and D11 should leave orders.count at 1.

likelyCause.text: The handler doesn't record the event id before it writes.

findings.caption: Same request, same response, a different state.
findings.measured: D5: HTTP 200 in 196 ms · orders.count 1 → 2, expected 1 · D11 (retry): HTTP 200 in 205 ms · orders.count 1 → 2, expected 1

findings.title: Over the 10 s budget for Stripe
findings.what: 2 of 8 valid invoice.paid deliveries took longer than the 10 s budget (Webhook Trap default): D10 (11 840 ms) and D16 (10 420 ms). Stripe doesn't publish its timeout, so these are over our default budget, not proven failures at Stripe.
findings.why: If Stripe times out waiting, the delivery counts as failed and is retried. Stripe doesn't publish the timeout. In this run, D10 went over our default budget, and the retry D11 created the duplicate order in F2.

citation.label: Stripe docs › Webhooks › Quickly return a 2xx response

fix.text: Acknowledge with 200 first, then queue the slow work. After the fix, D10 and D16 should respond within the budget.
fix.snippet:
res.sendStatus(200);            // acknowledge first
await queue.add('create-label', { invoiceId: event.data.object.id });

likelyCause.text: Only some deliveries of invoice.paid were slow, so the slow step is intermittent: usually an external call or a lock wait before the response.

findings.measured: D10 11 840 ms (+1 840 over) · D16 10 420 ms (+420 over) · median of the other 6 valid invoice.paid deliveries 202 ms

findings.title: Probe doesn't see subscription state
findings.what: Shuffled and Burst passed on orders.count. But customer.subscription.updated was delivered first in Shuffled (D6) and inside the burst (D15), and no probe reads subscription state.
findings.why: Out-of-order delivery usually breaks status fields, not counts.

fix.text: Add subscriptions.status to the probe in webhooktrap.yml. The next run then checks both.
fix.snippet:
probe:
  # keep your existing entries, then add:
  - as: subscriptions.status
    sql: select status from subscriptions where stripe_id = '{{subscription.id}}'

findings.measured: orders.count 0 → 1 after Shuffled and after Burst, expected 1 · subscription state not measured
